summary: A 1975 note on a change to the protocol between IMPs and hosts. It replaces RFC 687.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC sketches changes to the IMP/host protocol to support network growth. It allows old and new formats to run in parallel so hosts can transition gradually.

questions: how did arpanet support more than 63 imps
subtitle: Sketches an expanded IMP/host protocol with larger addresses and gradual compatibility.

tldr.problem: The IMP/host protocol needed room for network growth, including addressing hosts on more than 63 IMPs.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal expands the protocol leader and address field, adds message length and handling fields, and supports old and new formats in parallel.
tldr.outcome: RFC 704 revises RFC 687 and describes a backward-compatible transition plan with some exceptions.

today: RFC 704 obsoletes RFC 687. It sketches a protocol expansion and says a draft of the necessary changes to BBN Report 1822 was being produced.

sections.title: Why the Protocol Is Expanded
sections.content:
RFC 704 revises RFC 687 and sketches an expansion to the IMP/host and host/IMP protocol. One goal is to address hosts on more than 63 IMPs; the note says there were already 62 IMPs.

The authors aim to correct specific limits without changing the protocol's basic philosophy, because the short-term network needs do not allow massive fundamental changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol was near its limit on the number of IMPs. This note proposes an expansion while keeping the overall approach.

sections.title: Larger Leaders and New Fields
sections.content:
The leader is expanded from two to six 16-bit words, making room for additional or larger fields. The note discusses padding words between leaders so hosts with different machine word sizes can process messages without shifting data.

The address field is expanded to 32 bits. A new 16-bit field can optionally carry message length in bits, the maximum number of packets per message can grow from 8 to 16, and the handling type field is expanded to eight bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The larger leader provides room for expanded addresses and additional information. Padding can help hosts with different word sizes process it.

sections.title: Coexistence of Old and New Formats
sections.content:
The note proposes supporting old and new formats in parallel in IMPs for the foreseeable future. A host can tell its IMP which format to use through the format of its host-to-IMP NOP message and can switch modes for debugging.

A host using the old format cannot address hosts on IMPs numbered above 63. Where possible, IMPs will convert formats to allow old- and new-format hosts to communicate.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts can adopt the new format at different times. The IMP may convert between formats, although old-format hosts cannot address higher-numbered IMPs.

references.text: "IMP/Host and Host/IMP Protocol Change", RFC 687, revised by RFC 704.
